title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADRs
author: Maya Thompson
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's baseline architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding and code review, infrastructure (IaC and network), model-serving practices, observability, and performance benchmarking. It also indexes the canonical Decision Records (ADRs) relevant to these topics. Use this as the primary reference when designing new services, onboarding models, or drafting ADRs.

Goals
- Provide consistent, audit-able engineering practices across teams.
- Ensure production reliability and predictable performance for model inference.
- Reduce operational cost through standardized deployment and tuning patterns.
- Make decisions explicit and discoverable via ADRs.

1) API Standards

Intro
APIs exposed by Redwood services must be stable, discoverable, and easy to instrument. Public customer-facing APIs (Redwood API) and internal service-to-service APIs follow the same principles with different guardrails (rate limits, auth, SLA).

Key requirements
- Protocols: External APIs use HTTPS/REST+JSON. Internal high-throughput RPCs may use gRPC (see ADR-2024-11).
- Versioning: Use path versioning (/v1/, /v2/). Introduce new minor versions for incompatible changes. Maintain semver-style compatibility policy in API CHANGELOG.
- Authentication: OAuth2 / Bearer tokens for public; mTLS for sensitive internal paths and private deployments.
- Pagination: cursor-based pagination for collection endpoints (cursor, limit).
- Idempotency: POST operations that create resources must support an Idempotency-Key header.
- Error model: Use structured error responses: {"code": "SOME_CODE", "message": "human friendly", "details": [... ]}. Map HTTP codes to categories (4xx client, 5xx server).
- Rate limiting: Include RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset headers. Default quota policies live in product-pricing config.
- Telemetry: Emit per-request trace_id, model_id, model_variant, route, and customer_id (where applicable) to logs and traces.

OpenAPI & schema guidelines
- All public endpoints must have an OpenAPI (v3) spec checked into api-definitions/ and validated in CI.
- Keep request/response schemas explicit; avoid free-form objects except where necessary (use content-type: application/json).

Example error response (JSON)
{
  "error": {
    "code": "MODEL_NOT_LOADED",
    "message": "Requested model is queued for warmup",
    "retry_after_seconds": 30
  }
}

2) Coding Standards

Languages and style
- Primary languages: Go for high-throughput services, Python for orchestration and evaluation tooling, TypeScript for frontend/console, Rust for performance-critical components (where adopted).
- Follow language-specific style guides: gofmt/ goimports, black/flake8 for Python, eslint/prettier for TypeScript.

Testing and CI
- Unit tests required for new functionality. Target >= 80% coverage for critical packages.
- Integration tests: every service must include a minimal integration test that exercises RPC and critical code paths in CI.
- Performance regression tests are part of PR pipelines for runtime-affecting PRs (see perf-suite).

PR and review process
- Keep PRs < 400 lines where possible. For large changes, submit an ADR or design doc before implementation.
- Mandatory reviewers: code owner check in CODEOWNERS.
- Automate linting, security scans (Snyk or GitHub Dependabot), and static analysis (gosec, bandit) in CI.

3) Infrastructure & IaC Standards

Accounting and naming
- Resource naming follows: <env>-<team>-<service>-<component> (example: prod-rtp-serving-gpu-01).
- Tagging: All cloud resources must include tags: owner, team, cost_center, environment, project_id.

IaC practices
- Terraform is the canonical IaC tool. Maintain reusable modules in infra-modules/ with versioned releases.
- No direct console changes in production accounts; all changes via PR to terraform repo and deployment through CI pipeline.
- State management: use remote state with encryption (S3 + Dynamo lock on AWS, or appropriate cloud equivalents).

Network and security
- VPC design: separate subnets for control-plane, serving, and monitoring. Use NACLs and security groups with least privilege.
- KMS/HSM for key management (see private deployments docs).

Deployment patterns
- Blue/green or canary deploys for runtime services that affect inference paths. Canary policies should default to 5% traffic for 15 minutes for minor releases.
- Terraform applies must require CI approvals for prod.

4) Model-Serving Standards

Model packaging and onboarding
- Standard model package: manifest.yaml (model_id, version, architecture, input_schema, tokenizer, quantization_profile_id, performance_profile_id).
- All model packages stored in the model registry (artifact store) and referenced by immutable model_version identifiers.

Quantization and kernels
- Quantization profiles are defined in /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles and referenced by quantization_profile_id.
- Runtime must expose model_variant tags (fp16, int8, int4) and attach performance/accuracy profiles.

Cache and KV policies
- Prefix/KV caching enabled by default for long-running chat sessions. Cache TTLs, max_entries, and sharding configuration must be set per-model in manifest.

Autoscaling and capacity
- Autoscaling signals: GPU utilization > 65% sustained for 2m triggers scale-up; queue length (requests waiting > 200ms) sustained for 30s triggers scale-up faster.
- Reserved capacity (Dedicated) must be respected: do not autoscale below reserved pool thresholds.

Quality and rollout
- Canary model rollouts: start with 0.5% traffic, validate quality metrics (per prompt set) for 12-24 hours before increasing. Automatic rollback on quality regressions (see Redwood Optimize integration).

5) Observability Standards

Metrics & dashboards
- Core metrics (per service & per-model): request_rate, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms, error_rate, token_emit_rate, gpu_utilization, queue_length.
- Use standard metric names and tags: service, route, model_id, model_variant, region, env.
- Dashboards: per-service (overview), per-model perf, and customer-impact dashboards. Ownership for dashboards must be assigned in eng-platform.

Logging
- Structured JSON logs with fields: timestamp, level, trace_id, span_id, service, route, model_id, customer_id (where permitted), message.
- Sensitive data (PII) must be redacted before logs are persisted. Use the logging redact library and verify in CI.

Tracing & sampling
- Distributed tracing for request flows (OpenTelemetry). Default sampling rate 1% for non-prod and 10% for prod, with dynamic ramp-up for debugging.

Alerts and on-call
- Alert fatigue control: prefer SLO-derived alerts. See SLO section below for thresholds. Critical alerts must page oncall; informational alerts create tickets.

6) Performance Standards & Benchmarks

Latency & throughput targets (example baseline)
- Hosted small-sequence generate endpoints: p95 < 250ms for tokens < 64 for curated small models.
- Large-context chat (2k tokens): p95 < 1.5s under normal load for optimized model variants.
- Tail-latency: p99 should be < 3x p95 for steady-state workloads.

Benchmarking process
- All changes to the serving runtime that affect kernels, batching, or memory must be validated against the benchmarking-and-perf-suite (eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite).
- Benchmarks include microbenchmarks (kernel latency), end-to-end (inference latency under load), and cost-per-token calculations.

Load testing profiles
- Synthetic steady-state: 80% of expected daily QPS for 30 minutes.
- Spike test: 5x baseline for 5 minutes followed by graceful recovery.
- Long-tail test: low QPS with large sequence lengths to test memory and cache behavior.

Regression policy
- Performance regressions > 5% in cost-per-token or > 10% in p95 latency must block release until triaged. CI will mark performance-affecting PRs and run the perf-suite.

7) Decision Records (ADRs)

Index of recent ADRs relevant to architecture standards
- ADR-2023-04: Standardize on Terraform modules for multi-account infra (Decision: adopt shared modules with review gating). Owner: eng-infra.
- ADR-2024-11: gRPC for internal high-throughput RPCs (Decision: use gRPC with HTTP/2 for internal runtime-to-runtime communication; external APIs remain REST). Owner: eng-serving-runtime.
- ADR-2024-07: Quantization-first inference policy (Decision: default to FP16 for hosted; introduce int8 seeding for cost-sensitive workloads). Owner: applied-ml-and-evals.
- ADR-2025-01: Tracing sampling defaults and dynamic ramp (Decision: default prod sampling 10% with temporary ramp via feature flags). Owner: eng-platform.

Writing a new ADR
1. Create a short title and problem statement.
2. Provide alternatives considered and rationale (technical and business tradeoffs).
3. State the decision and the date.
4. List owners, mitigations, and follow-ups.
5. Add the ADR file under confluence/architecture-and-standards/adr-YYYY-NN.json and link to related pages.

ADR template (minimal)
- Title
- Status: accepted | rejected | deprecated | superseded
- Date
- Context
- Decision
- Consequences

8) Ownership and governance
- Every service and major dashboard must have a documented owner (team and primary owner). Ownership manifests are maintained in eng-platform/team-wiki.
- Standards are living documents. Major revisions require an ADR or a steering note; minor clarifications can be merged by eng-standards subteam.

Appendix: example checklist for onboarding a new model to production
1. Package model with manifest.yaml and upload to model registry.
2. Create or update performance_profile and quantization_profile.
3. Run end-to-end inference tests and perf-suite locally and in staging.
4. Submit a PR with model package and OpenAPI docs if public.
5. Perform canary rollout with quality metrics for 24 hours.
6. Promote to full traffic and monitor SLOs for 72 hours.
